items.question: How do you see reinforcement learning fitting into the broader idea of learning from experience?
items.object: Reinforcement learning as a way of learning from experience
items.answer: If I play football, for example, it looks very, very closely to reinforcement learning. I get a lot of times, and every time I adjust a little bit and see if it roughly matches what I wanted, and there is some self-reinforcement happening. When I learn mathematics, it's a very different type of thing. It's like reading about hard concepts and thinking about them very deeply inside my head until things click and I have them connected. Both of those in some way are learning from experience. They are just very different. We probably are spending the most compute than ever on learning from experience, but reinforcement learning is not the end of learning from experience, and there will be better approaches that researchers will be coming up with in the coming years on how to use that data.

items.question: What do you mean when you say that the first step to replacing Transformers is appreciating how far they have carried us?
items.object: Understanding Transformers as a first step toward replacing them
items.answer: Appreciating Transformer means understanding what it does well. So, if you're not solving the problems that it is solving well, you have to focus on its weaknesses. You have to understand good parts and bad parts. It's very easy in a lot of the work people are doing in architectures to try to make Transformers cheaper. They are trying to make Transformer more efficient. I very rarely see people thinking about how do we make Transformers more powerful, trying to do more express. But seeing someone's weak parts and strong parts are almost the same thing. It's just understanding the shape of Transformer a little bit more.

items.question: Why do you think model architecture is now the bottleneck to building smarter AI systems?
items.object: Model architecture as the bottleneck to smarter AI systems
items.answer: What I think right now, we are in this stage: we got really good at training really big models. We mastered two algorithms. We mastered pre-training at a large scale, and we mastered reinforcement learning at a large scale. And I'm asking myself a lot: what is next in machine learning? I think at this moment what the bottleneck is to better models and smarter systems is the architecture itself. It is this moment to revisit the train we've been riding for the last six years of trying to add more and more parameters to essentially two of the same operations, which are MoE and attention.

items.question: How does your experience using coding assistants shape the research you want to pursue at Core Automation?
items.object: Coding assistants as a guide to Core Automation's research agenda
items.answer: When I'm thinking about where we are today and what we are doing, I am thinking a lot about what Codex and what Cloud Code are doing for us. And I'm really appreciative of those systems, of the coding, of the workflow automation, and of the systems and products that we have today that we essentially have built over those six years of scaling. And I think this is the first step of thinking: if we want to work on the replacement, we need to see where we are, what problems we have solved, to start seeing what the next stage is, what problems we haven't solved yet, what kind of things are we missing. Whenever I use Codex and I am successful at a task, I also start thinking, why didn't I try to push that thing harder? Whenever I come to work, there are a lot of things I do with Codex, but I still come to work. I still ask it to do certain things for me. And I'm always asking myself, why am I even needed there? Core Automation's name and concept is that we want to be automating tasks. And why are those things not yet automated? Why is Codex not doing everything for me? And this is the question of the research, where we want to go. With that research, I'm trying to think: what kind of models, what kind of systems do we need, what kind of qualities do we need that we don't have today? And that's what I'm thinking a lot these days.

items.question: How did your experience scaling reinforcement learning at OpenAI change your understanding of what prevents models from solving real-world tasks?
items.object: Scaling reinforcement learning and the gap between benchmarks and real-world tasks
items.answer: What I think is the issue is that the models are being trained in the lab and are being deployed in the real world. That is the fundamental tension that is there. A bit of my disappointment comes from my personal story. Whenever we were starting the research and progress on scaling up reinforcement learning at OpenAI, I basically believed that scaling up reinforcement learning is a necessary stepping stone on a path to AGI since I started working at OpenAI. I was always a reinforcement learning maximalist. I always believed this is what we need to focus on. This is what we need to do. I've seen LLMs being scaled up to higher and higher levels through GPT-3 to GPT-4, and we're still doing very little RL. I had this internal belief that the moment we start scaling up RL, we'll solve everything. We'll be able to solve all the problems. And we eventually started scaling up RL. I was just in there. I was in the center of it. I was thinking, here we are. If you ask Jerry in 2024, when do we get AGI? I would say 2025 will be that year. This is where we solve everything. And I saw us training model after model. This model was getting better and better. All the benchmark scores were going up. And did we also solve all the real-world tasks at that moment? Unfortunately not. We still have work. And I realized there was this bit of distinction: all the benchmarks that we are evaluating our models on were essentially the same thing as we were training the models on. The evals and training side tasks are the same sides of the coin. But the real-world distribution and real-world task is much messier, much murkier, much more different. Our training data didn't really replicate the real-world use cases. And despite us basically maximizing all the tasks, if you ask anyone training models, “Hey, what is one of your main issues?” “I don't have hard enough tasks. I don't have what to train our model on.” Yet we are still not covering the entirety of the real-world distribution.

items.question: Why do you believe learning at test time requires a new algorithm expressed in the model architecture?
items.object: Architectural support for learning at test time
items.answer: My conclusion is we need to have models that learn at test time. We need to have models that learn with users on their data, on their real-world task, on the real-world distribution. And there are essentially two types of learning that we could be doing at test time. We could be doing in-context learning, essentially of transformers, which doesn't have fundamental problems of catastrophic forgetting. It doesn't have that issue. It is pretty data efficient. So that is great, but it's not very scalable. We only can have so much of it. It is limited and it has some more mechanical limitations of what actually are you doing when you build context. We have in-context learning, which is very limited and a very small amount of data. Whenever I'm using Codex, roughly after around 20 minutes of usage, I need to compact it and move it afterwards, which is not that much data. If all we can learn is for 20 minutes, it's not that much. And the second thing is fine-tuning. We could try to continuously fine-tune our models, but then those have the issues of catastrophic forgetting. We have issues of very low data efficiency. And neither of those are very solvable. Neither of those are very easy to find ways around. People have been trying. If they were easy to solve, someone already solved it. So my personal belief is we need to find an algorithm that we can meta-learn, that we can express on the architectural layer, that can represent how learning looks like, how learning looks like that can work on much longer horizons.

items.question: How do you understand the role of economics in making Transformers more successful to scale than LSTMs?
items.object: The economic advantage of Transformers over LSTMs
items.answer: I think those two things happened at the same time, but if anything happened there, it was mostly about economics, because technically you can scale up LSTMs. Just no one really dared to go in that direction. And they did scale much more poorly. In the scaling loss paper, there is a comparison of LSTMs and Transformers. And fundamentally, the scaling law of Transformers was better. There is a world where we never invented Transformers and we would be scaling LSTMs and we would be having some models. But because they would be much more expensive to train and much less impressive as a product, we would have just this worse experience and maybe no one would be able to convince people to spend as many dollars training those gigantic LSTMs because we wouldn't get a market return. The majestic thing about Transformer, which goes back to why we have to appreciate Transformers so deeply, is that Transformers are economically valuable. The cost of training them is lower than the revenue that they generate, which is the magic of machine learning and it's not guaranteed by itself. But for LSTMs it probably wouldn't be that way.

items.question: Why do you think testing new model architectures at small compute scales can miss their potential?
items.object: Evaluating new model architectures at small compute scales
items.answer: I think a lot of reasons why people didn't scale things before was because researchers before OpenAI had a lot of reluctance to scaling. It was often seen as unscientific, and research in algorithms was about how do we become more and more efficient? How do we, for the same compute budget, get better results? And it was a bit of a bet by OpenAI at that moment to say, “Hey, we don't care about better and better algorithms. We care about smaller and more scalable algorithms.” And how do we pour more and more compute and get better results, which OpenAI was criticized repeatedly by many people in the community for a long time. But thanks to that, we have the models that we have today. I think there are tons of architectures that can be scaled up. I am part of the Core Automations mission, and our belief is that a lot of architectural research happened at too small scale for too long. A lot of people are trying to say, “Hey, let's first try our architecture on a small data set in a small computer regime, and then see where it scales, only after you prove itself.” But for example, when you do work on reinforcement learning, you know that to get to any interesting results, you need a certain level of compute to even see the capabilities in a model. Reinforcement learning needs a baseline of ability to even start working. So where I am coming from, probably there are many architectures that need a baseline of compute to even start doing anything interesting and useful.

items.question: Why do you see starting a company as the right way to pursue alternatives to Transformers now?
items.object: Starting a company to research alternatives to Transformers
items.answer: I think in many ways it's likely a timing issue. The market is right now in a very specific place where the biggest and the most successful labs, by coincidence or by fate, are probably in the most competitive market fight ever right now, which makes them not very keen on trying different paths, trying alternatives. If Transformer is profitable and if you can spend more effort and more resources scaling Transformer to win in the next quarter, it's very hard to put a lot of attention and energy to work on something that will maybe be better or maybe will redefine the field in a year or two. So I think the biggest labs, and I talked to basically all of them, don't have that much interest in trying the alternatives to Transformer. And the labs that are not the biggest are doing whatever they can to do what the most successful labs are doing. And everyone is trying the same coding agent. If you look at last week's releases, everyone is trying to release a coding agent right now. And I think we need different paths and different approaches here. So that's the niche in the ecosystem we are trying to fill.

items.question: Where do you think transformer-based AI models top out?
items.object: The limits of transformer-based AI models
items.answer: I think it all comes back to what we are training transformers for and what we can do with them. We're doing pre-training, which is very good at distilling all the knowledge from the internet into transformers, and then we can RL them, through which we basically can bake all the workflows that we want into a transformer. Where Transformer has capped out is we have all the knowledge of humanity in the model together with the relationships and how they work together, how they can be combined. Basically, any task that we have training data for, we can put into the model, and we can have this gigantic model trained with a lot of compute on all the data in the world. And then if we ever stop training that model, what would happen? The question worth asking often and thinking about Transformer: what would happen if OpenAI and Anthropic stopped training new models and we got the Transformer we have today and said, “This is it. This is the best model we have”? Months pass, years pass, and the model is getting less and less useful. Maybe the lab really recorded every human on Earth, what they were doing, what their tasks were and their environments, and put them in the model, put them in the learning environment. But then what happens if any of that stuff changes? If there are new events in the world, if those new events have new relationships between them, if there are new types of tasks, new code bases, new tools to use, transformers are getting a lot of their usefulness and all value through things that are valuable having to be present in training. And when they are not, they suffer. There's some ability to adapt, but it's not very big and not very flexible. So in my mind this is the level where transformers top out, which in many ways is a tool to use for us. If there is a human who knows the limitations of a transformer, they can schedule that model, they can write a prompt for the task that you want. By doing the training we are doing, you can get very successful at that, and any task the model fails at, you get added to training data and the model can succeed. But that loop has to be the lab training the model for you. If the model fundamentally needs to be trained in the lab, how much do you think this is the goal, or would you want to be able to update the model somehow without having to go back there?

items.question: How do you understand what today’s pre-training is actually teaching models?
items.object: Pre-training as a way of learning
items.answer: I have this personal view that pre-training today is largely distilling other models into the new model, because most of the tokens on the internet are coming from AI. But there's clearly pre-training, which is behavioral cloning, mimicry, compression of internet data.

items.question: How do you see reinforcement learning fitting into the future of learning from experience?
items.object: Reinforcement learning and the future of learning from experience
items.answer: Reinforcement learning is not a particularly new approach, particularly a new thing to do. In some way, the age of experience has always been there. Reinforcement learning is not something that people haven't been thinking about or doing. Reinforcement learning was used to solve backgammon back in the day. They used to solve Go, StarCraft, Dota, and programming right now, and every time it comes down to the model writing its own experience and learning from that experience. But what I think is interesting and perplexing to people is that reinforcement learning is not really the only way to learn from experience, and there will be more. There will be a little bit more of, I think you can call it algorithmic, but essentially innovation in how we learn from experience. Just because reinforcement learning is only one way to do it. It's a mathematical formulation. Especially right now, how we are using it really likes those parallel rollouts for variance reduction and for comparing how the model does in parallel versions of the world, which is not how we learn from experience. We learn from our experience much more efficiently. We use those in many ways. At some moment I've been trying to explain to people how the brain learns. There's one learning algorithm in a brain. I think there are multiple, actually, and they work together. But if I play football, for example, it looks very, very closely to reinforcement learning. I kick the ball a lot of times, and every time I adjust a little bit and see if it roughly matches what I wanted, and I learn, or some self-reinforcement happens. When I learn mathematics, it's a very different type of thing. It's like reading about hard concepts and thinking about them very deeply inside my head until things click and I have them connected. Both of those in some way are learning from experience. They are just very different. So, summarizing my thinking of learning from experience: we've been doing it for a while. We probably are spending the most compute than ever on learning from experience, but reinforcement learning is not the end of learning from experience, and there will be better approaches that researchers will be coming up with in the coming years on how to use that data in richer new settings.

When I learn mathematics, it's a very different type of thing. It's like reading about hard concepts and thinking about them very deeply inside my head until things click and I have them connected. Both of those in some way are learning from experience. They are just very different. So, summarizing my thinking of learning from experience: we've been doing it for a while. We probably are spending the most compute than ever on learning from experience, but reinforcement learning is not the end of learning from experience, and there will be better approaches that researchers will be coming up with in the coming years on how to use that data in richer new settings.

items.question: How do you understand the purpose of automation at Core Automation?
items.answer: I think that automation—the version of automation by Core Automation—is about giving each human the maximum level of agency in some way. We're not trying to really get humans out of the loop, which is one version to automate, but it is about giving humans the ability to do the most with their amount of time. Whenever you are walking, you can get some distance. Whenever you get a bike, you can go a larger distance. Whenever you are in a car, you can go much, much larger. Whenever humans started farming, they had to farm by hand and work on a small plot of land. When you have a machine, you work on a much larger plot of land.

items.question: Why do you see building a new research lab around coding agents and automation as a promising way to advance deep learning research?
items.object: Building a research lab natively around coding agents and automation
items.answer: Personally, I am both a really great fan of the current coding agents and very happy it's, in some way, what I've been working for many years, both doing coding research and working on various versions of an AI scientist inside of OpenAI. In the end, I realized starting a company to realize that vision is one of the best ways to realize it, because the way you can do research today is very different. A single researcher can do much more. In the end, the speed of iteration, the speed of research, the speed of how quickly you can move through ideas and how quickly you can get data on your ideas is something very different. You can try to move the old structures around it, the teams, workflows, how data is gathered, or you can try to build natively for processes that maximally empower each researcher and allow them to iterate on their idea much quicker. We are here and we are trying to rebuild the deep learning stack and think how we can do almost each operation differently. What are various options? If we can execute even one of those experiments a day, that's already a pretty good iteration speed versus anything that was done before. There isn't really any fundamental law-of-physics reason why not. Maybe one day we get to 10 of those a day. Maybe one day we get 200 of those a day. Fundamentally, for that search process, optimization process, we should be able to find things that work in a better deep learning setting. What we are trying to do is—almost all of us are a team that is very agent-built and automation-built. We are trying to do an experiment: how far can we push those things, and how far can an organization that tries to do as much as we can with a small team get?

items.question: What would convince you that we've reached AGI?
items.answer: At some moment I used to say it's very much in everyone's heart, whatever they consider AGI. OpenAI says the system that can outperform all humans in economically valuable work, but it goes to my previous statement. What if OpenAI stops training models? Would that still keep working, and would that still keep the automation level the same, or would that drive? For me AGI is a model that can improve itself without a human in the loop in any way. That's the moment where we can meaningfully talk about AGI, because that is in some way a sub-definition of the previous one, because improving our models is actually a job that humans can do. It is economically valuable work. It definitely is the case, but removing humans from loops with models has been notoriously difficult so far. We haven't come anywhere close to it. It's very hard for me to find any task where we were able to get humans out of the loop. The human-LLM hybrid is really successful right now, but LLMs without humans, not so much, not at all. What I have seen there in 2024 and in early 2025 is that the current path doesn't get us there. I think we need some pretty serious research, at this company or some other, to try to unlock how we make our models learn and adapt at test time on a deeper level than we've been so far.

items.question: How are you approaching your lab’s search for an architecture that can continuously learn from deployment?
items.object: The search for a transformer replacement capable of continual learning
items.answer: We want to build models that continuously learn and then learn from deployment. We believe, as I mentioned, that transformers are incapable of continual learning. There's no way to put continual learning on transformers. So our quest is to find that new architecture, find that transformer replacement, and we want to build the most automated lab to do it. We want to be able to build experiments at scale the quickest we can, iterate on them, try a lot of new architectural ideas, have strong priors of what we want to do to search the space of architectures efficiently, to find that place faster than anyone else. That's what we want to do, and all the work we are doing on kernels, on large-scale training, on trying new architectural ideas, is exploring that space.

items.question: How will you know when you have found the continually learning architecture you are looking for at Core Automation?
items.object: Recognizing a successful architecture for continual learning
items.answer: There are always two angles. In my mind and my experience, every successful research had a plot that shows something that other plots don't show. There is one line that's bending in a different way, and you're saying this is what you want. But at least it is my experience with research: that plot is already quite late in a journey where most of the time you already know what you want and what you are up to. I am a bit joking, but it's actually true that all the best plots in my life I have done in a dream before they were real. I kind of knew what I was looking for. The question is when it actually clicks, if you know what I mean, because most of the time you kind of know what you are looking for, but you are not finding it. You try one thing and it doesn't work. Try a second thing and it doesn't work. But eventually all the right pieces fall into it, and most of those deep learning systems are very intricate. Usually you have to get five things right in a row for the thing to start working, and then eventually you get the plot that looks like you want, and then you know. So I think what we are looking for is systems that learn at test time and meaningful long-term adaptability of our systems. We are joking, but it's real: we want to be evaluating our systems in our everyday work. Will they get better at doing the work of Core Automation scientists each day?
